backups.name: North Slopes
backups.fa: James Tilton, railroad surveyor, August 1867 (he briefly named it 'Mt. Gregory Smith')
gear: helmet (loose rock and the short exposed summit step)
hazards: brief exposed Class 2-3 step/narrow ledge at the true summit
avalanche terrain on the peak's slopes when snow-covered
backups.overview: Denny Mountain rises directly above the Alpental ski area at Snoqualmie Pass, making it one of the most accessible summits in the corridor. Its long, jagged, roughly one-mile ridge runs NNW, with Alpental's ski runs (International, Edelweiss, Armstrong) climbing the peak's eastern flank; this route climbs those same runs and the slopes under the lift lines to the summit ridge. The scramble is little more than a steep grass/talus walk-up for most of its length in summer, but the true highpoint sits atop a short rock step — most parties (Mountaineers trip reports, trailhead logs) describe a brief, exposed Class 2-3 move or narrow ledge/chimney to actually tag the summit, so this isn't a pure Class 2 talus hike start to finish. USGS quad data puts the summit around 5,520+ ft (older NGVD29 datum); some newer survey accounts list it closer to 5,614-5,620 ft.
backups.beta: From the Alpental base area, ascend barren lower slopes to snowline, then follow the Lower International run and the steep, double-black-diamond Upper International run. From the top of Upper International, a wide ramp leads to a clump of alpine fir below the summit block; a steel cable protects a down-sloping, exposed rock-ledge traverse, followed by a short Class 2-3 scramble to the summit, which carries a radio tower and marker pole. Many parties descend a counterclockwise loop through Edelweiss Bowl and Midway Saddle, glissading Debbie's Gold back to the base.
backups.turnaround: Set a turnaround time based on the current avalanche forecast and how the snow is softening through the day, and avoid the exposed cable/ledge section near the summit if it is icy, wet, or visibility drops - a slip there is consequential.
backups.face: East flank, via the Alpental ski runs (Lower/Upper International)
backups.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.
obj_haz: avalanche/wet-snow slides on the ski slopes and Edelweiss Bowl
exposed, down-sloping rock ledge near the summit (cable-protected)
loose rock on the summit block
whiteout/featureless terrain on the open ski runs

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead Parking Lot
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required; from the lot cross the bridge near the restrooms and head uphill under the Sessel chairlift on the climbers'/goat path.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 Exit 52 and drive Alpental Road to the large lot at its end, roughly 3,100 ft. There is no signed trailhead or maintained trail for Denny itself — the route crosses the ski area base and follows climbers' and goat paths up the north-facing slopes.

waypoints.name: Base of Sessel Chairlift climbers' path
waypoints.note: Faint boot path marked with scattered pink/white/blue ribbons starts here; easy to lose in the overgrowth, so a GPS track is recommended.
waypoints.directions: Cross the bridge near the restrooms and head straight uphill under the chairline on the ski runs. The path is a boot track rather than tread, and route-finding rather than terrain is what stops parties down here.

waypoints.name: Upper meadows below Edelweiss Bowl
waypoints.note: Two steep open meadows climbed nearly straight up before the terrain steepens into rock.
waypoints.directions: Follow the boot track up through timber and brush. In summer expect stretches of slide alder, small hemlocks and huckleberry well over head height, loose scree underfoot, and flagging that starts and stops without reliably marking the line. The route goes nearly straight up rather than contouring.

waypoints.name: Edelweiss Bowl boulder field
waypoints.note: Meadow gives way to a rocky bowl beneath the old Edelweiss chairline; boulder-hop up the bowl toward the ridge saddle.
waypoints.directions: Above the second meadow the ground turns rocky beneath the old Edelweiss chairline. In a lingering snowpack parties climb the International ski runs on firm snow instead, with axe and crampons, converging at the top of the old lift station.

waypoints.name: Saddle atop Edelweiss Bowl
waypoints.note: Top out on the saddle and turn left (south) along the ridge toward Denny's summit block.
waypoints.directions: Boulder-hop up the bowl on the most stable line you can pick out; the top of the bowl is the saddle, roughly where the old chairline unloaded.

waypoints.name: Summit block chimney / exposed ledge
waypoints.note: Steep class 3 finish - either a vertical chimney or an exposed ledge traverse around a tree - loose rock and real exposure on the final scramble.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the open ramp toward the summit horn runs a couple hundred feet, changing from scree and heather into broken rock. Keep the party spread out — everything on this stretch is loose.

waypoints.name: Denny Mountain Summit
waypoints.note: Tight, rocky high point with room for only a few people; views across Alpental bowl to Snoqualmie Pass and the Alpine Lakes Wilderness.
waypoints.directions: Both finishes go. The chimney is about eight feet and stiff enough that packs often come off; the ledge line instead ducks behind the tree on the left and traverses around to a short final scramble. A cable handline is in place along that ledge and the slab above it — treat it as balance, not as an anchor. The ledge is down-sloping and often slick, so it is the option that punishes wet rock.

sectionBreakdown.note: From the Alpental (Snow Lake) parking lot, follow climber/goat paths uphill under the Sessel chairlift, pick up a faint boot path through timber, and continue to the boulder fields…

backups.detailed_rack: Not a roped climb for most parties; an ice axe and crampons are the primary tools for the snow slopes, and some parties carry a short sling/handline as backup on the cable-protected ledge below the summit.
pro_tips: One of the most accessible summits at the pass
Many parties do it as a snow climb in late spring/early summer (after the resort closes but before the snowpack melts off), which allows a glissade descent via Debbie's Gold
A helmet is worth carrying for the short rock step near the highpoint
watch_out: a short, exposed Class 3-ish move is needed to actually tag the true summit — don't assume the whole route is a casual Class 2 walk
in winter/spring, I-90 and the Alpental turnoff can be affected by WSDOT avalanche-control closures on this same mountain
backups.pro_needs: No fixed protection beyond the resort-installed steel cable on the final ledge; a rope is not typically used but could be carried for extra security on that section.
backups.approach: Park at the large Alpental Ski Area lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 1.4 miles/2 miles up from I-90 Exit 52, per differing trip-report odometers), elevation roughly 3,100 ft. There is no signed trailhead or maintained trail for Denny Mountain itself — climbers cross the base area and pick up boot-track/climber's paths under the old Armstrong Express / Sessel chairline on the mountain's north-facing slopes. Early season or in a lingering snowpack this is straightforward: hike the barren lower ski slopes for a few hundred feet of gain to snowline, then switch to crampons/axe and follow the Lower International ski run up into a small basin. From there the route continues up the steep Upper International run (a double-black-diamond pitch that holds firm snow late into the year and is the crux of the ascent in spring conditions) to the top of the Edelweiss chairlift unloading station (the Edelweiss lift was rebuilt as a new Doppelmayr triple chair, opened January 2026, replacing the original 1967 Riblet double that had earned it the old 'Edelweiss' nickname on this route). In summer/dry conditions the same line goes as a rough boot-path and talus/scree scramble through brush, small hemlocks, and huckleberry — expect neck-deep slide alder and bramble in spots, loose scree underfoot, and only intermittent pink/white/blue flagging that does not reliably mark the line; route-finding is the main hazard low on the mountain. Above the lift station, angle up the wide open ramp toward the summit horn; this transitions from scree/heather to broken rock. A fixed steel cable (a short via-ferrata-style handline) protects an exposed, down-sloping and often slick rock ledge traverse just below the top. The route finishes with a short Class 2–3 scramble (some parties note a stiffer Class 3–4 move) through a narrow rock cleft to the summit block, which carries an old radio-relay structure and a survey marker. One-way distance/gain from the lot to the summit runs roughly 2.3–2.4 miles and about 2,500 ft, consistent with the ~4.7 mi (7.56 km) round-trip logged for this route; best window is late spring through mid-July after the resort closes but before the snow gullies melt out and expose looser rock and scree.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or typically used on the standard North Slopes route. Reverse the summit cleft and cable-protected ledge back down to the top of the Edelweiss lift station (rebuilt as a new triple chair in January 2026), taking care on the down-sloping ledge traverse (it is more exposure-sensitive descending than ascending). From there, most parties drop into Edelweiss Bowl rather than exactly retracing the International runs: descend the open bowl, cross east through Midway Saddle, and finish down Debbie's Gold ski run back to the base area, glissading or boot-skiing the snow where conditions allow — this is faster than downclimbing the steep Upper International pitch and is the descent line most parties use (roughly 1.3 hours down versus 2.5–2.7 hours up). In low-snow/summer conditions without a glissade path, simply reverse the ascent line of least resistance back through the ski-slope brush and scree to the base lodge, watching for loose rock and the same route-finding ambiguity encountered on the way up. Hazards on descent are exposure on the cable ledge, potential glissade-path hazards (rocks, run-out onto talus) in Edelweiss Bowl, and loose/scree footing lower down; no technical rope work is needed on this route.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward down the open ski-slope terrain at almost any point below the summit horn; the only committing section is the fixed-cable ledge traverse just under the top - downclimb it carefully or wait it out rather than pushing through in poor conditions.

itinerary.cal: Goes on firm snow from late spring to mid-July, and as a dry scramble from mid-July into September; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at Alpental in summer, a Sno-Park pass in winter.

days.note: From the Alpental (Snow Lake) parking lot, follow climber/goat paths uphill under the Sessel chairlift, pick up a faint boot path through timber, and continue to the boulder fields in Edelweiss Bowl below the summit ridge. The final summit block is class 3 with an optional short class 4 chimney (or a ledge traverse around a tree to the left as an alternative); descend by reversing the same route, with some parties glissading lower snow patches when present.

days.objective: Summit Denny Mountain and return same day

itinerary.totalNote: A single, moderately strenuous day: roughly 4.5-7 hours car-to-car with about 2,500 ft of gain over ~4.7 miles round trip, culminating in a class 3 (optional class 4) summit block.

access.fees: $5 daily or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass (Interagency/America the Beautiful pass also honored); no wilderness permit needed since this route stays outside the adjacent Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Note Summit at Snoqualmie charges separate paid lot parking (roughly $25/vehicle) during active ski-area operating days in winter.
access.notes: Climbable roughly April–September; heavy winter snowfall and frequent avalanche control closures on I-90 affect access the rest of the year.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; stay clear of lift infrastructure and any operating ski terrain
access.permit: None required — free self-issue day-use permit at the trailhead (no quota for day use).
access.closures: Respect ski-area operations and closures in winter; WSDOT periodically closes I-90 through the pass for avalanche-control work on Denny Mountain's own slide paths, which can affect access even at the trailhead
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Snoqualmie Ranger District (Alpental ski area operates on NF land under a special-use permit)
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Snoqualmie Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass ($30/yr) or America the Beautiful pass, or a $5/day pass at developed trailheads.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass at the Alpental trailhead lot

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

road.name: Alpental Road (Forest Road 9040)
road.status: Paved, plowed and open year-round to the Alpental ski area base lot; not seasonally gated for vehicle access.
road.driveNote: From I-90 Exit 52 (West Summit), turn north under the freeway and take the second right onto Alpental Road; it's about 1.3-1.5 paved miles to the large lots at the ski-area base. Paved and plowed to the resort year-round.
road.seasonalGate: Not gated, but access can be affected by WSDOT avalanche-control closures of I-90 itself in winter/spring

climate.fall: Increasingly wet and cold with the first snows returning to the upper slopes; shortening daylight.
climate.spring: Lingering, often wet/heavy snowpack on the upper mountain into June; best window for a firm-snow ascent but avalanche conditions must be checked.
climate.summer: Snow-free by mid-to-late summer, exposing loose scree, brush, and rock that make the route notably more tedious than in spring.
climate.winter: Heavy, wet snowfall and high avalanche danger; the mountain's flanks host the Alpental ski area during this period.
climate.typical: Wet, maritime Cascade-crest climate at Snoqualmie Pass — one of the snowiest highway corridors in the state, so shaded north-facing terrain like this route can hold snow into July. Denny Mountain's own slopes are one of three named avalanche paths WSDOT monitors and controls along I-90 through the pass.

bySeason.spring: Snow-covered; popular as a spring snow climb after the resort closes but before snowpack melts off
bySeason.summer: Best dry-scramble window; slopes clear of snow except lingering patches early season

emergency.notes: Very accessible from the pass with reasonable cell coverage near the trailhead, weaker higher on the ridge.
emergency.rangerStation: Snoqualmie Ranger District, Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — 902 SE North Bend Way, Bldg 1, North Bend, WA 98045, (425) 888-1421
emergency.nearestHospital: Snoqualmie Valley Hospital, 9801 Frontier Ave SE, Snoqualmie, WA 98065 — 24-hour ER, (425) 831-2300; Level 5 trauma / Level 3 stroke center, roughly 25 minutes from the Alpental trailhead
emergency.sheriffDispatch: King County Sheriff's Office (dial 911 for emergencies; SAR missions coordinated through KCSO)

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekend mornings July-August, when Alpental parking and the Snow Lake trailhead corridor are busiest
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Roughly a dozen or so documented parties per season (occasional trip reports spanning 2004-2024); light, because the line goes up the ski runs and under the Sessel chairlift rather than on a marked trail

fitnessSpec.hiking: Moderate — roughly 2000-2500 ft gain over a short summer approach; round trips from the Alpental lot run about 3 to 6.5 hours depending on snow and brush
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day pack (water, layers, helmet); no overnight or technical gear needed in dry conditions

partner_requirements.approachTime: Short — roughly 1-1.5 hours from the Alpental trailhead to the base of the north-facing slopes
requiredSkills: Basic off-trail route-finding (goat/climber paths under the ski lift, no maintained tread)
Comfort on loose talus/scree and boulder fields (Edelweiss Bowl area)
Awareness of and courtesy around active ski-area infrastructure (lift towers, cables)
No rope/technical skills required for a dry-season ascent, but comfort on a short exposed Class 3 step
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Mostly Class 2 scramble with a short, exposed Class 3 summit step; suitable for a partner new to off-trail scrambling but comfortable with loose, unmarked terrain

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late spring to mid-July as a firm-snow ascent after the resort closes; mid-July through September as the driest window for the snow-free scramble

July.reason: Slopes usually dry out by mid-to-late July; early July can still hold lingering snow patches on north-facing terrain

August.reason: In season; driest, most stable footing and lowest snow risk

October.reason: Early season snow and increasing rain become likely at the pass as fall progresses; ski-area preparations and shoulder-season closures may apply

September.reason: Still reliably dry; shortening days and cooling temps

weather.typical: Very wet maritime climate at Snoqualmie Pass; the July-October window is the drier season, with slopes clear of snow and best conditions in August
weather.probability: Occasional afternoon thunderstorms possible in July-August; rain frequency increases into October as the pass transitions toward its wet season

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Mostly low-to-moderate consequence Class 2 terrain with a short, exposed Class 3 summit step; primary hazards are loose footing on scree/talus and boulder fields and proximity to ski-area infrastructure (lift towers/cables) that the route travels alongside

avalanche.zone: Snoqualmie Pass forecast zone. On the spring snow ascent the ski runs, gullies and Edelweiss Bowl are avalanche terrain and are no longer controlled once the resort closes; once the slopes are snow-free, usually from mid-July, there is no avalanche hazard

byMonth.May: Real hazard on the snow ascent, rising with warming and wet-snow slides; check the forecast and start early
byMonth.June: Wet-snow slide hazard remains in the gullies and Edelweiss Bowl while snow lingers; check the forecast
byMonth.April: Real hazard while the slopes are snow-covered; the closed ski area is no longer controlled, so check the Snoqualmie Pass forecast

gaps: No precise per-season party-count data found; crowd estimate is inferred from sparse, irregular trip-report frequency (2004, 2010, 2017, 2021, 2022, 2024) rather than a hard count
No dedicated NWAC zone or avalanche product exists specifically for this route's dry-season climbing window; zone naming is inferred from the general Snoqualmie Pass forecast area
No official/guidebook partner-skill certification found beyond general Class 2 scrambling conventions
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead (~3,100 ft), at the end of Alpental Road off I-90 Exit 52

backups.rope_note: Class 3 scramble typically approached via Alpental ski area/Source Lake; ice axe and helmet required per Mountaineers guidance, microspikes/crampons recommended if snow is firm.

approach_variants.name: Alpental base area and the ski runs under the old Armstrong Express line
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the large Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road, about 3,100 ft. There is no signed trailhead and no maintained trail for Denny Mountain. Cross the base area and pick up boot tracks and climbers' paths on the north-facing slopes under the old Armstrong Express and Sessel chair lines.

On snow this is simple: walk the barren lower slopes a few hundred feet to snowline, put on crampons and axe, and follow the Lower International run into a small basin, then the steep Upper International run — a double-black pitch that holds firm snow late and is the crux in spring — to the top of the Edelweiss chairlift unloading station.

Dry, the same line is a rough boot path and scree scramble through slide alder, small hemlocks and huckleberry, with only intermittent flagging that does not reliably mark anything.

About 2.3 to 2.4 miles and 2,500 ft one way.
approach_variants.season: Late spring to mid-July, after the resort closes but before the snow gullies melt out and expose looser rock and scree
hazards: Loose footing on scree and dirt once the snow has gone
Neck-deep slide alder and bramble low on the mountain in summer, with unreliable flagging
A brief exposed class 2-3 step and narrow ledge at the true summit
Avalanche terrain on these slopes when snow-covered
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This peak gives you man-made landmarks, which is unusual and worth using. Navigate by the ski runs and the lift, not by the mountain: Lower International, then the steep Upper International, then the top of the Edelweiss chairlift unloading station. Standing at that lift station is the arrival test for the end of the approach, and it is a building — it does not disappear in cloud.

Where the real climbing begins: above the lift station, angle up the wide open ramp toward the summit horn, which changes underfoot from scree and heather to broken rock.

The unmistakable marker is a fixed steel cable. A short via-ferrata-style handline protects an exposed, down-sloping and often slick ledge traverse just below the top. There is nothing else like it on this mountain. If you have reached steep ground and there is no cable, you are not on the correct line to the summit block.

And the top confirms itself: past the cable, a short class 2-3 scramble through a narrow rock cleft reaches a summit carrying an old radio-relay structure and a survey marker. Hardware on the summit is the final proof.

The hard part, honestly stated: on dry ground the route-finding low on the mountain is the hazard, not the summit. The flagging is pink, white and blue, inconsistent, and does not reliably mark the line. In snow this problem disappears entirely, which is why the season here is spring rather than summer.

climbing_route.label: Open ramp to the summit horn
climbing_route.notes: Above the Edelweiss lift station, angle up the wide open ramp toward the summit horn, transitioning from scree and heather to broken rock.

climbing_route.label: Cabled ledge traverse
climbing_route.notes: A fixed steel cable — a short via-ferrata-style handline — protects an exposed, down-sloping and often slick rock ledge traverse just below the top.

climbing_route.label: Rock cleft to the summit block
climbing_route.notes: A short scramble through a narrow rock cleft finishes the route; some parties report a stiffer class 3-4 move. The summit block carries an old radio-relay structure and a survey marker.
